why.correct: The electronegativity differences are O–H 3.4 − 2.2 = 1.2, N–H 0.8, C–Cl 0.6 and C–S 0.0. The largest difference gives the most unequal sharing, so O–H is the most polar.
options: Cl is very electronegative, but so is C compared with H: the C–Cl difference is only 3.2 − 2.6 = 0.6. Polarity depends on the difference, not on one atom.
Right: a difference of 1.2 is the largest of the four.
The N–H difference is 3.0 − 2.2 = 0.8, smaller than the O–H difference of 1.2.
C and S both have an electronegativity of 2.6, so this bond is the least polar of the four. Larger atoms do not make a bond more polar.

why.correct: 3.4 − 1.3 = 2.1. A difference this large, between a metal and a nonmetal, means the bond is ionic.
C and S have the same electronegativity, 2.6, so neither nucleus pulls the shared electrons harder: the bond is nonpolar covalent.
options: H and Br differ by 0.8, the largest difference of these four pairs.
N and O differ by 3.4 − 3.0 = 0.4, so O pulls the shared electrons a little harder. Two nonmetals next to each other in a period still differ.
H and C differ by 0.4, so the sharing is slightly unequal.
Right: a difference of 0.0 means equal sharing.

why.correct: O (3.4) is more electronegative than S (2.6). The shared electrons spend more time near O, so O is δ− and S is δ+.
options: Right: the electron density shifts toward the more electronegative atom.
Total electron count does not decide where the shared pair sits; the pull of each nucleus on the bonding electrons does, and O pulls harder.
Two nonmetals share electrons, but they share them unequally unless their electronegativities match. S and O differ by 0.8.
Lower electronegativity means a weaker pull on shared electrons, so S ends up with less of the electron density, not more.

why.correct: KCl is a metal with a nonmetal, so it is ionic: K⁺ cations and Cl⁻ anions held in a regular pattern, each ion next to ions of opposite charge. That is Box 1.
options: Box 3 shows separate units of two identical atoms sharing electrons, which is a covalent element such as Cl₂, not an ionic compound.
Box 2 shows identical metal cations among free electrons, which is a metal. KCl has no free electrons.
Right: alternating cations and anions.
Neither picture has both cations and anions; an ionic compound must show both kinds of ion.

why.correct: In a metal, the atoms give up their valence electrons to a shared sea, leaving cations in a regular pattern with the electrons moving among them. Box 2 shows exactly that.
options: Box 3 shows separate two-atom units of a nonmetal. Sodium atoms do not pair up into molecules.
Box 1 has anions as well as cations. Pure sodium has no anions, because every atom is the same element.
Right: metal cations in a sea of electrons.
Box 1 shows an ionic compound; only Box 2 fits a pure metal.

why.correct: Both atoms are Cl, so their electronegativity difference is zero. Each nucleus attracts the shared pair equally: a nonpolar covalent bond.
options: Right: identical atoms share equally.
Transfer needs a large electronegativity difference. Two identical atoms have none, so neither can pull an electron away from the other.
Unequal sharing needs two atoms of different electronegativity; two Cl atoms are identical.
In Box 3 the electrons belong to separate two-atom units, not to a sea spread over the whole sample.

why.correct: Box 2 is metallic bonding: cations in a sea of delocalized electrons, held together by the attraction between the cations and that electron sea.
options: Right: the electrons are not tied to one atom or one bond.
That describes a covalent bond. In a metal the electrons move among many cations.
Right: the Coulombic attraction between the cations and the electron sea is the metallic bond.
That describes an ionic compound such as Box 1. A metal has no anions.
A large difference describes ionic bonding. A metal is made of one element, so there is no difference at all.

why.correct: In a covalent bond two atoms share a pair of electrons; both nuclei attract that pair, and that attraction holds the atoms together.
options: An electron pair attracted by only one nucleus does not hold two atoms together, so it is not a bond.
That is an ionic bond: the attraction between oppositely charged ions.
That is metallic bonding, with delocalized electrons.
Right: a shared pair attracted by two nuclei.

why.correct: Calcium is a metal and fluorine a nonmetal with a very different electronegativity, so Ca gives up electrons and the compound is made of Ca²⁺ and F⁻ ions.
options: N and F are both nonmetals, so they share electrons in polar covalent bonds.
Right: a metal with a nonmetal.
C and S are both nonmetals with almost the same electronegativity; the bonds are covalent.
Si is a metalloid, not a metal, and Cl is a nonmetal; they share electrons, so SiCl₄ has polar covalent bonds.

why.correct: Coulomb's law: Na's 3s electron sits in the third shell, shielded by 10 core electrons, so Na has a low ionization energy. Cl has a high effective nuclear charge for its valence shell, so it attracts an added electron strongly. Moving the electron gives Na⁺ and Cl⁻, which then attract each other.
options: Atoms do not want or choose anything. The cause is the strength of the attractions, which this option leaves out.
Right: the explanation compares the attraction in both atoms.
Electrons repel each other; Cl attracts the added electron because of its nuclear charge and short distance, not because it already has many electrons.
Size matters because of distance from the nucleus, and this option skips that reasoning; 'room' is not a cause.

why.correct: Differences: Cl–Cl 0.0, C–H 0.4, O–H 1.2, Na–F 3.1. Bond character is a continuum: the larger the difference, the more ionic the bond.
H–Cl (1.0) and C–O (0.8) join two nonmetals of different electronegativity, so the electrons are shared unequally.
options: Right: two nonmetals that differ by 1.0.
Right: two nonmetals that differ by 0.8.
Identical atoms share equally, so Cl–Cl is nonpolar covalent.
Na is a metal and the difference is 2.3, so Na–Cl is ionic.

why.correct: Down group 17 the halogen's valence electrons are in higher shells, farther from the nucleus, so it pulls on shared electrons less strongly. The bond stays one shared pair but becomes less polar.

variables.name: Electronegativity difference between H and the halogen
variables.why: Electronegativity falls down a group (F 4.0, Cl 3.2, Br 3.0), and H stays at 2.2, so the difference shrinks from 1.8 to 0.8.

variables.name: Size of the partial positive charge on H
variables.why: A smaller electronegativity difference shifts less electron density away from H, so its δ+ is smaller.

variables.name: Number of electrons shared between H and the halogen
variables.why: Each bond is one shared pair of two electrons; only how evenly the pair is shared changes.

why.correct: A dipole arrow points toward the more electronegative atom, where the electrons spend more time (δ−). The crossed tail, like a plus sign, sits at the δ+ end. F is far more electronegative than H.
options: H does give up electron density, which is exactly why the arrow points away from it, toward F.
That drawing points toward H, which would mean H is δ−. F is the more electronegative atom.
Two different nonmetals still share unequally; H–F differs by 1.8, one of the most polar covalent bonds.
Right: toward F, plus-shaped tail at H.

why.correct: MgO is ionic (Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ attract each other). Copper contains Cu cations too, but the negative charge holding them together is a sea of delocalized electrons, not anions: metallic bonding.
options: Right: what balances the cations decides the bond type.
Positive ions appear in both ionic and metallic bonding; the difference is whether anions or delocalized electrons hold them.
Mg is a metal, but in MgO it has given its electrons to O, forming O²⁻ anions; that is ionic bonding.
In MgO electrons are transferred, and in copper they are delocalized; neither is a shared pair between two atoms.

why.correct: The bond length is the distance at the curve's minimum, where the potential energy is lowest. Curve 2's minimum is at about 74 pm.
options: 436 is the depth of the minimum in kJ/mol, an energy, not a distance.
Right: the x-coordinate of the minimum.
At 30 pm the nuclei would be pushed together so hard that the energy is far above zero; that is not where the atoms settle.
At 400 pm the curve is nearly flat at zero: the atoms are hardly interacting, so this is not a bond length.

why.correct: Separating the atoms means climbing from the minimum (about −240 kJ/mol) to zero, where the atoms no longer interact. That takes about 240 kJ per mole: the bond energy.
options: Zero would mean the atoms are already free. Energy is released when a bond forms; breaking it is the reverse, so about 240 kJ must be added.
About 199 is the distance in pm at the minimum, read from the wrong axis.
The climb is from about −240 to 0, which is 240 kJ, not twice that.
Right: the depth of the well.

why.correct: Closer than the bond length, the repulsion between the positive nuclei (and between the electron clouds) grows faster than the attraction, so the energy climbs.
options: Right: repulsion wins at short distance.
Nothing breaks: the atoms are pushed too close together. Breaking a bond means moving to the right, toward large distances.
Coulomb's law says attraction gets stronger, not weaker, as the distance shrinks. It is the repulsion that grows even faster.
The valence electrons stay; the rise comes from charges of the same sign being forced close together.

why.correct: The shared electrons of Cl₂ are in n = 3, much farther from each nucleus than H's 1s electrons, and Cl's core electrons repel at short range. The minimum energy is reached at a larger separation: 199 pm against 74 pm.
options: Mass alone does not set bond length; the number of occupied shells (distance from the nucleus) does.
Two nuclei repel each other; they do not attract. More protons do not pull atoms apart.
Right: atom size, set by the occupied shells, sets the bond length.
Weaker and longer often go together, but one does not cause the other here; both follow from Cl's larger size.

why.correct: 0.250 mol × 436 kJ/mol = 109 kJ. The moles cancel, leaving kJ; three significant figures.
C–C 154 pm and 347 kJ/mol; C=C 134 pm and 614; C≡C 120 pm and 839. More shared pairs: shorter and stronger.
options: The energies rise from 347 to 839 kJ/mol, so the bonds get stronger.
The lengths fall from 154 to 120 pm, so the bonds get shorter, not longer.
Right: both trends from the table.
The energy more than doubles from single to triple.

why.correct: A double bond places two shared pairs between the nuclei. More negative charge between them means a stronger attraction to both nuclei, so the minimum of the potential energy curve sits at a shorter distance (123 pm against 143 pm) and is deeper.
options: Right: more shared electrons, stronger attraction, shorter bond.
The atoms' cores are unchanged; what changes is how much electron density sits between the nuclei.
If it were two bonds each half as long, the double bond would be 72 pm. The table shows 123 pm.
The double bond is stronger (745 against 358 kJ/mol); its potential energy minimum is lower, which means more energy is needed to break it, not less room.

why.correct: 1.00 mol × 945 kJ/mol − 1.00 mol × 160 kJ/mol = 945 kJ − 160 kJ = 785 kJ.
Deeper means a larger bond energy (839 against 347 kJ/mol); farther left means a shorter bond length (120 against 154 pm).
options: Both the length and the energy differ, so the minimum moves.
Farther right would mean a longer bond, but C≡C is shorter.
Shallower would mean a weaker bond, but C≡C is stronger.
Right: stronger and shorter.

why.correct: Adding a shared pair between the same two atoms shortens and strengthens the bond; the atoms' nuclei do not change.

variables.name: Bond length
variables.why: Six shared electrons attract the two nuclei more strongly than four, pulling them closer: 125 pm to 110 pm.

variables.name: Energy needed to break 1 mol of the bonds
variables.why: The stronger attraction makes a deeper potential energy well: 418 kJ/mol to 945 kJ/mol.

variables.name: Number of protons in each nitrogen nucleus
variables.why: Bonding involves the valence electrons only; each nucleus still has 7 protons.

why.correct: "Intra" means within. An intramolecular force acts between the atoms inside one particle, such as a covalent, ionic or metallic bond.
options: That attraction acts between separate molecules, not within one. Unit 3 covers those forces.
Right: a bond inside one molecule.
Gravity on a whole sample is not a force between atoms within a particle.
A push on container walls comes from particles hitting them, not from bonding within a particle.

why.correct: Separate atoms are at zero potential energy; at the bond length H₂ is at −436 kJ/mol. Moving to lower potential energy releases the difference, for example as heat. Bond formation releases energy; bond breaking requires it.
options: This is the most common sign mistake: it is breaking a bond that takes energy. Forming one releases energy.
Right: forming a bond lowers the potential energy.
The atoms are the same, but their arrangement and attractions change, and so does the potential energy.
As the atoms approach, a bond forms; nothing breaks.

why.correct: Coulomb's law: the force is proportional to q₁q₂/r². The product of the charges is 2 × 2 = 4 for Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ against 1 × 1 = 1 for Na⁺ and F⁻, and r is smaller (210 against 231 pm). Both factors make the Mg²⁺–O²⁻ attraction stronger.
options: The charges are different (1+ and 1− against 2+ and 2−), so the attractions differ.
Electronegativity is about attracting shared electrons in a bond, not about the attraction between two ions. Use the charges and the distance.
Mass does not appear in Coulomb's law; charge and distance do.
Right: the answer compares both charge and distance for both pairs.

why.correct: 431 kJ/mol × 1000 J/kJ = 431,000 J/mol; 431,000 J/mol ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol = 7.16 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per molecule.
The bond energy is the energy needed to take the atoms from the bottom of the well back to zero, where they no longer interact: the depth of the minimum.
options: Right: the depth of the well.
That distance is the bond length, not the bond energy.
At very short distances the energy is high because the nuclei repel; that height is not the bond energy.
That is a distance on the x-axis; bond energy is read on the energy axis.

why.correct: Both compounds have ions of charge 1+ and 1−. F⁻ (133 pm) is smaller than Cl⁻ (181 pm), so the ion centers are closer (231 against 282 pm). By Coulomb's law the attraction is stronger, the lattice energy is larger, and more energy is needed to melt the solid.
options: NaF is ionic: no electrons are shared between Na and F. Compare the ions' charges and the distance between them.
Right: same charges, shorter distance, stronger attraction.
Mass does not set melting temperatures of ionic solids; the Coulombic attraction between the ions does. MgO is lighter than CaO and also higher-melting, but because of distance, not mass.
F⁻ and Cl⁻ have the same charge, 1−. The difference is size.

why.correct: The distances are close (210 and 231 pm), so the main difference is charge: 2+ and 2− against 1+ and 1−. The product of the charges is 4 against 1, so by Coulomb's law the attraction, and the lattice energy, are several times larger.
options: Both have two ions per formula unit (Mg²⁺ + O²⁻, Na⁺ + F⁻).
Mg²⁺ is smaller, but the distances differ only by about 10% (210 against 231 pm); that cannot explain a 1900 °C difference on its own. The doubled charges do.
A smaller electronegativity difference would make a bond less ionic, not more. The difference comes from the ions' charges.
Right: the charge product (4 against 1) dominates.

why.correct: The 1+/1− compounds come first, with the longer distance weaker: KCl (315 pm) < NaCl (282 pm). The 2+/2− compounds are far larger: CaO (240 pm) < MgO (210 pm). The melting temperatures follow the same order.

A full-credit Coulomb's-law argument compares both species: the same charges, a larger cation, a greater distance between ion centers (315 against 282 pm), and so a weaker attraction and a lower melting temperature.
options: Right: it names the charges, the sizes for both ions and the effect on attraction.
"Bigger compound" is vague. It does not name the ion distance or the attraction, which a reader needs to see.
The extra electrons are inner shells around K's own nucleus; the reason is the larger distance between ion centers.
An ionic solid is not made of molecules. The attraction is between ions throughout the lattice.

why.correct: In the solid the ions sit in a repeating three-dimensional array, each ion surrounded by ions of opposite charge. Box 1 shows one layer of that.
options: Box 3 shows separate Na–Cl pairs, as if NaCl were made of molecules. An ionic solid has no separate pairs: each ion attracts all its neighbors.
Box 2 shows ions spread out without a regular pattern, which is the melted (liquid) salt.
Right: alternating ions in a regular array.
Box 3 is not a correct model of an ionic solid; only Box 1 is.

why.correct: Charge is carried in an ionic compound by moving ions. When the solid melts (Box 2) the ions can move past each other toward the oppositely charged ends of the circuit. In the solid (Box 1) the same ions are locked in the lattice.
options: Box 2 in fact shows fewer ions than Box 1. The number of ions is not the issue; whether they can move is.
Melted salt does not contain free electrons; the moving charges are the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions themselves.
Right: mobile ions carry the current.
Box 1 also contains ions. They just cannot move.

why.correct: NaCl is a lattice, not a collection of molecules. Each Na⁺ is surrounded by several Cl⁻ ions (and each Cl⁻ by several Na⁺), all attracting it; no Cl⁻ belongs to one particular Na⁺. The formula NaCl gives the 1 : 1 ratio, not a molecule.
options: Right: the attraction extends through the whole array.
The ratio in Box 3 is 1 : 1, which is correct for NaCl; the problem is the isolated pairs.
Na⁺ has 10 electrons and Cl⁻ has 18, and Cl⁻ is in fact larger. The drawing gets the sizes right.
This is the misconception the item targets: ionic compounds do not form discrete molecules.

why.correct: Its four nearest neighbors in the layer are all Cl⁻. In the real three-dimensional solid there is also one above and one below the layer, so each Na⁺ in NaCl has six Cl⁻ neighbors; the diagram shows one layer.

In the crystal each ion has opposite-charge neighbors. A small shift of one layer brings cations beside cations and anions beside anions; the repulsion pushes the layers apart and the crystal splits. This is why ionic solids are brittle.
options: The attractions in an ionic solid are strong: salt melts at 801 °C. It is brittle because shifting a layer creates repulsion, not because the forces are weak.
NaCl is held by ionic bonds between ions, not by covalent bonds.
The ions keep their electrons; the crystal splits because of how the ions are rearranged.
Right: like charges line up and repel.

why.correct: Ions carry the charge, so the compound conducts only when its ions are free to move: melted, or dissolved in water.
options: In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice, so no charge can flow.
Right: melting frees the ions to move.
Right: in water the ions separate and move independently.
A powder is still made of tiny solid crystals; the ions are still fixed.

why.correct: An ionic solid is a lattice of alternating cations and anions held by Coulombic attraction throughout.
options: Ionic compounds do not form discrete molecules; the formula only gives the ratio of ions.
Right: the definition of an ionic solid.
That describes a metal.
That describes a solid held together by covalent bonds, a different kind of solid.

why.correct: Al³⁺ (3+) and O²⁻ (2−) give the largest charge product, and both ions are small. Coulomb's law predicts the strongest attraction; aluminum oxide melts above 2000 °C.
options: Mg²⁺ has a 2+ charge, but Cl⁻ is only 1− and larger than O²⁻.
Right: the highest charges with small ions.
Both ions are singly charged, and Br⁻ is large.
Both ions are singly charged and both are large, so KI has the smallest lattice energy of the four.

why.correct: Going down group 1 the cation grows while its charge stays 1+, so the attraction to F⁻ weakens. LiF melts at about 850 °C, CsF at about 680 °C.

variables.name: Distance between cation and anion centers
variables.why: Cs⁺ has its outermost electrons in the fifth shell, Li⁺ in the first, so Cs⁺ is far larger and the ion centers sit farther apart.

variables.name: Lattice energy
variables.why: Same charges, larger distance: by Coulomb's law the attraction, and so the lattice energy, decrease.

variables.name: Charge on the cation
variables.why: Li and Cs are both in group 1 and form 1+ ions.

why.correct: To melt, ions must leave their fixed places. Each ion is held by strong Coulombic attraction to several neighbors throughout the lattice, so a lot of energy is needed.
options: Density does not explain melting temperature; the strength of the attraction between the particles does.
NaCl has ionic bonds between ions in a lattice, not covalent bonds within molecules.
Free-moving electrons describe a metal; the electrons in NaCl stay on their ions.
Right: many strong attractions in every direction.

why.correct: KI is ionic: strong attractions make it hard with a high melting temperature, a shifted layer makes it brittle, and fixed ions mean no conduction until it melts or dissolves.
options: Right: the typical ionic-solid properties.
Bending and conducting as a solid are properties of metals.
Strong attractions between ions give ionic solids high melting temperatures (KI melts at 681 °C).
It is the other way round: the melted salt conducts because its ions can move.

why.correct: In an interstitial alloy, much smaller atoms (here carbon) fit into the gaps between the larger metal atoms, which stay in their usual places. Box X shows that: steel.
options: Box W is pure iron: one kind of atom only.
Right: small atoms in the holes of the iron lattice.
In Box Y the second element's atoms take the places of iron atoms; that is a substitutional alloy.
Box W is a pure metal and Box Y is substitutional; neither has atoms in the gaps.

why.correct: A substitutional alloy forms when the added atoms are about the same size as the host atoms, so they can take their places in the lattice. Cr (128 pm) is almost the same size as Fe (126 pm); stainless steel contains chromium this way.
options: Ca (197 pm) is far larger than Fe, so it does not fit in an iron atom's place.
K (227 pm) is far too large to replace Fe in its lattice.
B (84 pm) is much smaller than Fe; small atoms fit between the iron atoms instead, as in Box X.
Right: nearly the same radius as Fe.

why.correct: A metal bends because its layers of atoms can slide past one another, with the electron sea holding them together throughout. Small atoms wedged between the layers act like pins: the layers catch on them and resist sliding. The metal becomes harder, stronger and less malleable.
options: Right: the interstitial atoms block the layers from sliding.
The harder alloy is still held by metallic bonding; the change comes from the atoms blocking movement, not from fewer electrons.
The carbon atoms do not change the size of the iron atoms.
The carbon atoms sit in a metallic lattice; steel is not an ionic compound.

why.correct: Pure iron and both alloys are metallic solids: cations in a sea of delocalized electrons, so all three conduct and all are held by metallic bonding.
options: Right: the electron sea is present in all three.
Right: alloys keep the metallic bonding of their main metal.
Only Box W is a single element; X and Y are alloys, mixtures of elements.
Only Box X has atoms in the gaps; in Y the second element replaces iron atoms.

why.correct: Box Y has 20 atoms, 5 of them the second metal: 5 ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%.
Zn (134 pm) and Sn (151 pm) are close enough in size to Cu (128 pm) to take the places of Cu atoms in the lattice; neither is small enough to fit in the gaps.
options: Larger atoms cannot fit into the small gaps between metal atoms.
Only much smaller atoms, such as C, fit into the gaps; Zn and Sn are not much smaller than Cu.
Right: similar sizes, so they substitute.
An alloy is a mixture of a metal with another element, often another metal, as here.

why.correct: Bronze (95) is harder than brass (70), which is harder than pure Cu (50). Sn (151 pm) differs from Cu (128 pm) much more than Zn (134 pm) does, so each Sn atom distorts the layers more and makes sliding harder, even though bronze has far fewer added atoms (7% against 30%).
options: Brass (70) is softer than bronze (95), so the claim contradicts the data.
Bronze has fewer added atoms (7%) than brass (30%), yet is harder, so the amount alone cannot be the reason.
Right: the size mismatch, not the amount, fits the data.
Bending tells you they are still malleable; the hardness numbers range from 50 to 95.

why.correct: In a metal the cations are held by delocalized electrons that move with them. When a layer slides, each cation is still surrounded by the electron sea, so the bonding is kept. In an ionic solid a shift brings like charges together and they repel.
options: Right: the electron sea follows the cations.
Copper and its alloys are held by metallic bonding, not covalent bonds.
Metals contain cations, which would repel each other if the electron sea were not between them.
A thin ionic crystal still snaps; thickness is not the reason.

why.correct: Pure copper and both alloys are metallic solids. Their delocalized electrons are free to move, so they flow as a current when a voltage is applied.
options: Shared pairs are held between two atoms and cannot carry a current through the solid.
Metals contain cations but no anions, and their cations stay in place; it is the electrons that move.
None of these alloys has small atoms in the gaps (Zn and Sn substitute for Cu), and pure copper conducts too.
Right: mobile electrons carry the current.

why.correct: Malleability comes from layers sliding without breaking the metallic bond: the delocalized electrons surround the cations wherever they move.
options: Gold melts at over 1000 °C, so its bonding is not weak; it is malleable because its layers can slide.
Right: sliding layers held by the electron sea.
The cations are closely packed; it is sliding, not empty space, that lets the metal change shape.
Metallic bonding is not one bond between two atoms: each cation is attracted to the electron sea around it.

why.correct: Carbon atoms are small, so they sit in the gaps between iron atoms (an interstitial alloy). They block the layers from sliding, which makes the steel harder and less malleable.
options: Blocking the layers makes sliding harder, not easier.
Right: the interstitial atoms pin the layers.
Steel is still metallic and still has delocalized electrons, so it conducts.
Steel is harder but still a metal; it bends before it breaks, unlike an ionic crystal.

why.correct: Small atoms make an interstitial alloy: the lattice of the host metal is kept, but the extra atoms in the gaps resist sliding.

variables.name: Hardness
variables.why: N atoms are much smaller than Fe, so they fit in the gaps and block the iron layers from sliding.

variables.name: Malleability
variables.why: With the layers pinned, the metal bends less easily before it breaks.

variables.name: Number of iron atoms in each layer of the lattice
variables.why: In an interstitial alloy the host atoms stay where they are; the small atoms go between them, not in place of them.

why.correct: An alloy is a mixture: its composition can vary (brass may be 60-80% copper), and it keeps metallic bonding and metallic properties.
options: Metals form cations, not anions; in an alloy the atoms keep sharing a sea of electrons.
An alloy is a mixture with a variable composition, not a compound with a fixed formula.
Melting and cooling a pure metal leaves it pure; an alloy has a second element.
Right: a metallic mixture.

why.correct: Both are metallic solids with delocalized electrons, which carry electric current and also carry energy quickly through the solid.
options: Right: delocalized electrons carry charge.
Right: the mobile electrons also carry energy, so metals feel cold and heat up quickly.
Alloys are mixtures with variable composition, so they have no single fixed formula.
Metals and alloys are malleable; brittleness is typical of ionic solids.

why.correct: Cu is about 11% smaller than Ag; atoms this close in size replace host atoms. Only much smaller atoms (such as C, N or B) fit in the gaps between metal atoms.
options: Right: the size match decides.
Being somewhat smaller is not enough to fit in the gaps between atoms; the gaps are far smaller than a Cu atom.
The amount of an element does not decide where its atoms go; their size does.
Group membership is not the reason; the similar atomic radii are.

why.correct: N₂ has 2 × 5 = 10 valence electrons. Diagram 3 shows a double bond (4) and four lone pairs (8), which is 12. The correct diagram is a triple bond with one lone pair on each N: 6 + 4 = 10.
options: HCN has 1 + 4 + 5 = 10: one single bond (2), a triple bond (6) and one lone pair (2). It is correct.
Right: 12 electrons drawn for a 10-electron molecule.
H₂CO has 2 + 4 + 6 = 12: two C–H bonds (4), a C=O bond (4) and two lone pairs (4). It is correct.
BF₃ has 3 + 21 = 24: three bonds (6) and nine lone pairs (18). It is correct, with an incomplete octet on B.

why.correct: B has three bonds and no lone pairs: 3 × 2 = 6 electrons. Boron has only three valence electrons, so in BF₃ it ends with six, an incomplete octet. This is one of the known exceptions to the octet rule.
options: Period 2 atoms such as B cannot have more than eight electrons; expanded octets start in period 3.
Not every atom has an octet: H has 2, and B commonly has 6.
Six around B is allowed; the diagram uses exactly 24 electrons and each F has an octet.
Right: three bonding pairs, six electrons.

why.correct: Only O carries lone pairs: two of them. C has four bonding pairs (two to H and a double bond to O) and no lone pairs.
Count every bonding electron around C: H–C contributes 2 and C≡N contributes 6. 2 + 6 = 8, an octet, with no lone pairs on C.
options: Right: two bonding electrons plus six.
The diagram shows no lone pairs on C and a triple bond to N.
The C–N bond is triple, not double, and C has no lone pair.
C has eight electrons around it; incomplete octets are typical of B, not C.

why.correct: S 6 + 4 × O 6 = 30, plus 2 for the 2− charge = 32 electrons.
B 3 + 4 × H 1 = 7, plus 1 for the 1− charge = 8 electrons. Four B–H bonds use all 8, giving B an octet.

NO has 5 + 6 = 11 valence electrons, an odd number. Electrons in a Lewis diagram come in pairs, so one electron is left unpaired and one atom has fewer than eight. NO is an odd-electron species (a free radical).
options: BH₄⁻ has 8 electrons: four B–H bonds give B an octet, and each H has its 2.
PCl₃ has 26 electrons: three P–Cl bonds, a lone pair on P and three on each Cl gives every atom an octet.
Right: an odd total cannot be all pairs.
SO₄²⁻ has 32 electrons and can be drawn with an octet on every atom (four S–O single bonds).

why.correct: Six bonding pairs put 12 electrons around S. Atoms in period 3 and below can hold more than eight valence electrons (an expanded octet). Each F has one bond and three lone pairs: an ordinary octet.
options: SF₆ is a real, stable gas; period 3 atoms can exceed the octet.
Both electrons of a bonding pair count for each atom it joins.
Right: six bonds, 12 electrons, period 3.
Each F has exactly 8 (one bond, three lone pairs); F is in period 2 and cannot expand.

why.correct: A lone pair (nonbonding pair) is a pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom and is not shared.
options: Right: an unshared pair of valence electrons.
Two shared electrons are a bonding pair, drawn as a line.
Lewis diagrams show valence electrons only; core electrons are left out.
An unpaired electron is a single dot, found in odd-electron species.

why.correct: Count, skeleton, outer octets, leftovers on the center, then multiple bonds if the center is short. Check at the end that the diagram uses exactly the counted number of electrons.
CO₂ has 4 + 2 × 6 = 16 electrons. Two double bonds (8) and two lone pairs on each O (8) use all 16, and every atom has an octet.
options: That uses 8 + 2 + 4 = 14 electrons and leaves the single-bonded O short of an octet.
That uses 4 + 12 = 16 electrons but leaves C with only four electrons; lone pairs on O must become double bonds.
That uses 4 + 12 + 4 = 20 electrons, four more than CO₂ has.
Right: 16 electrons, octets everywhere.

why.correct: NH₄⁺ has 5 + 4 − 1 = 8 electrons. Four N–H bonds use all 8, so there is no lone pair. The student added an electron for the charge instead of removing one.
options: Two lone pairs would make the count even larger, 12 electrons.
Right: the 1+ charge removes an electron.
In NH₃ nitrogen has a lone pair, but in NH₄⁺ that pair has become the fourth N–H bond.
H holds two electrons, one bonding pair; it never needs eight.

why.correct: P in PCl₅ makes five bonds: 10 electrons around a period 3 atom. The others have eight or fewer around the central atom.
options: Right: five bonding pairs, 10 electrons.
C has four bonds, exactly an octet.
N has three bonds and a lone pair, exactly an octet; period 2 atoms cannot expand.
B has three bonds and no lone pair: six electrons, an incomplete octet, not an expanded one.

why.correct: Valence electrons: 5 + 3 × 7 = 26. Three N–Cl bonds use 6, leaving 20 electrons = 10 lone pairs: three on each Cl (9) and one on N.
H forms only one bond, so it sits on the outside. In acids that contain oxygen, the H is attached to an O, and O (which forms two bonds) links H to Cl. The skeleton is H–O–Cl.
options: In acids that contain oxygen, the H is bonded to O, and H–O–Cl gives every atom an octet without any charges.
Right: O in the middle, H on the end.
H holds two electrons, one bond, so it cannot be a central atom.
Every atom in a molecule is connected; an unbonded H would make it two separate species.

why.correct: CN⁻ has 4 + 5 + 1 = 10 electrons. A triple bond (6) and one lone pair on each atom (4) use 10, and both atoms have octets.
options: That uses 2 + 12 = 14 electrons, four more than the ion has.
That uses only 6 electrons and leaves both atoms short.
That uses 4 + 8 = 12 electrons, two more than the ion has.
Right: 10 electrons, two octets.

why.correct: N has 5 valence electrons. In Structure I it has two lone pairs (4 electrons) and one double bond (4 bonding electrons, half is 2). 5 − 4 − 2 = −1.
O: 6 valence electrons − 2 in its one lone pair − 3 (half of the 6 in the triple bond) = +1.

Formal charges: I is O 0, C 0, N −1; II is O −1, C 0, N 0; III is O +1, C 0, N −2. I and II both have small formal charges, but II puts the −1 on O (3.4), the more electronegative atom, which holds extra electron density best.
options: Symmetry is not a rule for choosing; Structure I puts the −1 on N, which is less electronegative than O.
Right: smallest formal charges, negative on the most electronegative atom.
Structure III has the largest formal charges (+1 and −2), and puts a positive charge on O. A triple bond does not make up for that.
Size is not the test; electronegativity is. N is less electronegative than O, so the −1 belongs on O.

why.correct: In any valid Lewis diagram the formal charges add up to the overall charge (−1 here), and every structure for OCN⁻ must show all 16 valence electrons.
options: Right: I is 0 + 0 − 1, II is −1 + 0 + 0, III is +1 + 0 − 2.
Right: each one shows 8 bonding and 8 lone-pair electrons.
An ion with a −1 charge must have at least one atom with a nonzero formal charge.
In all three, C has four bonding pairs and no lone pair.

why.correct: When several valid diagrams differ only in electron placement, the real ion is a single resonance hybrid: one structure with the electrons delocalized. The best diagram (II) contributes most, so the hybrid is closest to it.
options: Every ion in the sample has the same hybrid structure; there is no mixture of different ions.
The ion does not flip between structures; it has one real structure that no single diagram shows.
Each valid diagram is a resonance structure; the less favorable ones contribute less, not nothing.
Right: one hybrid, weighted toward the best diagram.

why.correct: A single diagram predicts two different bonds, but both measure 128 pm, between a single and a double bond. Ozone has two equivalent diagrams; the real molecule is their hybrid, with each O–O bond of bond order 1.5.
options: Right: equal, intermediate lengths are the evidence for resonance.
Both bonds really are the same length; that is what the single-diagram picture fails to explain.
With two double bonds, ozone's 18 electrons would put 10 around the central O, which period 2 atoms cannot hold; each bond is in between.
The molecule does not flip; it has one structure, the hybrid.

why.correct: Total bond pairs between C and the three O atoms: 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Spread over three equal bonds: 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33.
Bond order 1 (methanol, 143 pm) is longest, 2 (formaldehyde, 121 pm) shortest, and 4/3 (carbonate, 129 pm) lies in between.
options: No single diagram has three double bonds; the hybrid has 4/3 for each bond.
A higher bond order means more shared electrons and a shorter bond, not a longer one.
Right: higher bond order, shorter bond, and fractional orders fit between.
The table shows the link clearly: bond order goes up as length goes down.

why.correct: Fewer bonds sharing the extra pair gives each bond a larger share: formate's bonds are bond order 1.5, carbonate's 1.33.

variables.name: Bond order of each C–O bond
variables.why: Formate shares 3 bond pairs over 2 bonds (3/2 = 1.5); carbonate shares 4 over 3 (4/3 ≈ 1.33).

variables.name: Length of each C–O bond
variables.why: A higher bond order means more shared electrons between the nuclei and a shorter bond (formate C–O is about 127 pm).

variables.name: Number of atoms bonded to the central C atom
variables.why: Carbonate's C is bonded to three O atoms; formate's C is bonded to two O atoms and one H atom: three in both.

why.correct: Formal charge compares the electrons an atom brings (valence) with the electrons assigned to it in the diagram: all of its lone-pair electrons and half of each bond.
options: This ignores the atom's valence electrons, which every formal charge starts from.
That counts both electrons of every bond for the atom; a bond is shared, so the atom gets half.
Right: the formal charge formula.
That is the formula with the sign reversed; it gives +1 where the true formal charge is −1.

why.correct: C: 4 − 2 − 3 = −1. O: 6 − 2 − 3 = +1. The diagram is still the best one because it is the only one that gives both atoms an octet; formal charge is a bookkeeping tool, not the real charge.
options: Right: computed from the diagram, with both octets kept.
A neutral molecule needs formal charges that add to zero, not formal charges that are each zero: −1 + 1 = 0.
That is what electronegativity would suggest, but the formula gives the opposite for this diagram.
Each atom has one lone pair (2) and half of six bonding electrons (3): the values are −1 and +1.

why.correct: S: 6 valence − 0 lone-pair electrons − ½ × 8 bonding electrons = +2. Each O is 6 − 6 − 1 = −1, and +2 + 4(−1) = −2, the ion's charge.
The double bond can be drawn to any one of the three O atoms, giving three diagrams that differ only in electron placement.

Resonance structures keep every atom in the same place and differ only in where the electrons (double bonds and lone pairs) are drawn. The two nitrite diagrams move the double bond from one O to the other.
options: Rotating a drawing gives the same diagram, not a second resonance structure.
Moving the H to a different atom changes which atoms are bonded, so these are different molecules, not resonance structures.
Changing the central atom changes the skeleton; resonance never moves atoms.
Right: same atoms, different electron placement.

why.correct: O=C=O: O 6 − 4 − 2 = 0, C 0, O 0. O≡C–O: triple-bonded O 6 − 2 − 3 = +1, C 0, single-bonded O 6 − 6 − 1 = −1. Diagrams with formal charges closer to zero are preferred, and the measured C–O bonds in CO₂ are equal.
options: Formal charge, not the strength of one bond, is how we compare diagrams; this one also puts +1 on an O atom.
Right: all-zero formal charges win.
It does put −1 on an O, but it also puts +1 on the other O; a diagram with no formal charges is better.
Octets are necessary but not enough; when both diagrams have octets, compare the formal charges.

why.correct: In NO₃⁻ the double bond can sit on any of three O atoms, and in O₃ on either end O. Each set of diagrams is equivalent.
options: Right: three equivalent structures.
Right: two equivalent structures.
H₂O has only single bonds and one valid diagram; there is no double bond to move.
CH₄ has four single bonds and one diagram.

why.correct: N has four electron domains: three bonds and one lone pair. They point to the corners of a tetrahedron; with one corner taken by the lone pair, the atoms form a pyramid with N at the top.
options: Trigonal planar needs three domains and no lone pair, like BF₃. NF₃'s lone pair is a fourth domain.
Right: four domains, one of them a lone pair.
Trigonal bipyramidal needs five domains with no lone pairs, as in PCl₅; N has only four domains.
Tetrahedral is the electron-domain arrangement; the molecular geometry names only the atoms' positions.

why.correct: Shape comes from the number of electron domains. B has three (trigonal planar, 120°). N has four, one a lone pair, so the domains are arranged tetrahedrally and the atoms form a trigonal pyramid.
options: All the bonds in both diagrams are single bonds.
Electronegativity affects polarity, not the number of domains that sets the shape.
B is in fact larger than N; size is not what decides the shape here.
Right: the lone pair is the difference.

why.correct: Cl has five domains (three bonds, two lone pairs) in a trigonal bipyramidal arrangement. The two lone pairs take equatorial positions, where they have more room, leaving the three F atoms in a T shape.
options: Right: five domains, two lone pairs.
Trigonal planar has three domains and no lone pairs; Cl has five domains.
Trigonal pyramidal has four domains with one lone pair; Cl has five domains.
A seesaw has five domains with only one lone pair, as in SF₄.

why.correct: Every bond is polar (F is more electronegative than each central atom). In NF₃ (pyramidal) and ClF₃ (T-shaped) the bond dipoles do not cancel. BF₃ (trigonal planar) and XeF₂ (linear, lone pairs around the middle) are symmetrical, so their bond dipoles cancel.
options: Right: the pyramid's dipoles add up to a net dipole.
Right: the T shape is not symmetrical, so the dipoles do not cancel.
The three B–F dipoles point 120° apart in a plane and cancel.
The two Xe–F dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel; the three lone pairs sit evenly around Xe.

why.correct: Xe has five domains: two bonds and three lone pairs. The three lone pairs sit in the equatorial plane, 120° apart, and the two F atoms take the axial positions, opposite each other: a linear molecule.
options: 109.5° belongs to four domains; Xe has five.
120° separates equatorial positions, where the lone pairs are, not the F atoms.
Right: the F atoms are axial, opposite each other.
90° separates an axial from an equatorial position; both F atoms are axial.

why.correct: C2 has three electron domains: the double bond to C1 (one domain), the single bond to C3 and the bond to H. Three domains: sp².
options: sp³ means four domains; C2 has only three, because a double bond counts as one.
sp means two domains, as at C3 (a single bond and a triple bond).
Right: three domains.
An atom has one hybridization set by its total number of domains; it is not assigned bond by bond.

why.correct: Every single bond is σ. A double bond is 1 σ + 1 π; a triple bond is 1 σ + 2 π. C1=C2 gives 1 π and C3≡N gives 2 π: 3 π bonds.
One σ bond for each pair of bonded atoms: C1–H, C1–H, C1–C2, C2–H, C2–C3, C3–N. That is 6 σ bonds.
C3 has two electron domains (the single bond to C2 and the triple bond to N, which counts as one). Two domains point opposite each other: linear, 180°.
options: Right: two domains, linear.
120° fits three domains, as at C2.
109.5° fits four domains; a triple bond is one domain, not three.
90° occurs only with five or six domains.

why.correct: All three have four electron domains (tetrahedral arrangement). A lone pair is held by one nucleus only, so it spreads out closer to the central atom and pushes the bonding pairs together: 109.5° with none, 107° with one, 104.5° with two.
options: Bond length does not set the angle between the bonds here; repulsion between domains does.
Electronegativity is not what sets these angles; the number of lone pairs is.
Fewer atoms do not fill space; lone pairs take the place of the missing bonds and push the others together.
Right: lone pairs take up more room than bonding pairs.

why.correct: BH₃ has no lone pair, so its three domains spread out to 120° in a plane (trigonal planar). NH₃'s lone pair is a fourth domain: the arrangement is tetrahedral and the H–N–H angle closes to about 107°.
options: Bond repulsion due to electronegativity is a small effect; the lone pair is the main difference.
Right: three domains against four.
Total electron count does not set the shape; the number of domains on the central atom does.
Bond length does not set the angle; the number of domains does.

why.correct: Each central atom has four electron domains (bonds plus lone pairs: 4 + 0, 3 + 1, 2 + 2), so each is sp³. Hybridization counts domains, including lone pairs.
options: That counts only the bonds. Lone pairs are domains too.
Right: four domains each.
NH₃ and H₂O have lone pairs that make up their four domains.
sp needs two domains, as in CO₂.

why.correct: CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O all have four domains arranged tetrahedrally, but the molecular geometry names the atoms only. Only CH₄, with no lone pairs, has its atoms at the four corners of a tetrahedron.
options: Right: four bonding domains and no lone pairs.
The domains are tetrahedral, but with one lone pair the atoms form a trigonal pyramid.
The domains are tetrahedral, but with two lone pairs the atoms form a bent shape.
BH₃ has three domains and is trigonal planar.

why.correct: Polarity depends on bond polarity and shape. Each C=O bond is polar (O is more electronegative), but in a linear molecule the two dipoles point in opposite directions with equal size, so the net dipole is zero.
options: C in CO₂ has no lone pairs: its four bonding pairs are in the two double bonds.
O (3.4) is more electronegative than C (2.6), so each bond is polar.
A double bond between different atoms is polar; the electrons are pulled toward O.
Right: the shape makes the dipoles cancel.

why.correct: SO₂ has 18 valence electrons; S has two bonding domains and one lone pair, three domains in all. With one domain a lone pair, the O–S–O shape is bent (about 119°).
options: Right: three domains, one a lone pair.
CO₂'s C has two domains (two double bonds) and no lone pairs: linear.
Be in BeCl₂ has two bonds and no lone pairs: linear.
C in HCN has two domains, a single and a triple bond: linear.

why.correct: C has four domains, arranged tetrahedrally; every pair of positions is 109.5° apart, so the two C–Cl dipoles (larger than the C–H ones) add to a net dipole whichever two corners they occupy.
options: No lone pairs does not make a molecule nonpolar; CH₂Cl₂ has unequal bond dipoles that do not cancel.
A flat Lewis drawing is not the 3-D shape. The molecule is tetrahedral, not square planar.
Right: the real 3-D shape decides, and no arrangement cancels the dipoles.
The molecule's polarity does not depend on how it is drawn; in 3-D every arrangement is the same.

why.correct: Valence shell electron pair repulsion: bonding pairs and lone pairs are regions of negative charge that repel, so they take positions as far apart as possible.
options: Electronegativity affects bond polarity, not the direction the bonds point.
Mass plays no part in VSEPR; the repulsion of electron domains does.
Right: domains spread apart to reduce repulsion.
Real angles are 180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90° and in-between values, depending on the number of domains.

why.correct: Fewer domains means a wider angle: sp³ (four domains, 109.5°) in CH₄, sp (two domains, 180°) in ethyne.

variables.name: Number of electron domains on the carbon atom
variables.why: Each C in ethyne has a bond to H and a triple bond to C, two domains; C in CH₄ has four.

variables.name: Bond angle around the carbon atom
variables.why: Two domains spread to 180° (linear), wider than 109.5° for four domains.

variables.name: Number of valence electrons the carbon atom brings
variables.why: Carbon has four valence electrons in every compound; only how they are used in bonds changes.
